content.title: First Crewed Moon Mission Since 1973 Is ‘Go’ For 2026  — What We Know
content.text: Artemis II will send astronauts around the moon in February-April 2026, marking NASA’s first crewed lunar mission in 50+ years and paving the way for future crewed lunar landings.gettyAre you ready for NASA’s most significant human spaceflight in a generation? Originally planned for September 2025 and now slated for February 2026, the space agency’s landmark Artemis II mission will carry astronauts around the moon for the first time since 1972, sending humans back into deep space and setting the stage for future lunar landings. Launching amid new leadership at NASA and renewed political emphasis on exploration, Artemis II is going to be in the headlines a lot in 2026. Here’s everything you need to know about it.Why Does Artemis II Matter In 2026?Artemis II is NASA’s first crewed mission beyond low Earth orbit since Apollo 17, which saw astronauts Eugene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt depart the moon’s surface on Dec. 7, 1972 — 53 years ago. In a press release on Dec. 16, the agency described the mission as a critical step toward “a human return to the lunar surface in preparation to send the first astronauts — Americans — to Mars.” The success of Artemis II would demonstrate that NASA’s next-generation spacecraft and rocket systems are ready to safely carry humans into deep space.The mission also arrives during a leadership transition. Newly sworn-in NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has pledged to “return American astronauts to the Moon, establish an enduring presence on the lunar surface, and laying the groundwork to deliver on President Trump’s vision of planting the Stars and Stripes on Mars.” A routine SpaceX mission to the International Space Station in February 2026 aside, Artemis II will be the first major human spaceflight conducted fully under Isaacman’s tenure. NASA's Space Launch System (SLS) and Orion spacecraft, with a full moon, at Launch Complex 39B at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida on June 14, 2022 prior to the Artemis I mission.NASA/Ben SmegelskyNASA’s Artemis II Mission And What It Will DoArtemis II will be a crewed lunar flyby, not a landing. Four astronauts will travel aboard NASA’s Orion spacecraft on a free-return trajectory that loops around the moon and brings them back to Earth without requiring major propulsion burns. Artemis II will be a 10-day mission with two orbits of Earth before moving into a highly elliptical orbit. After a trans-lunar injection (a maneuver that sends a spacecraft on a trajectory to orbit the moon) 24 hours later, the crew may experience a brief total eclipse of the sun as the moon passes between them before traveling at least 5,000 nautical miles (9,300 kilometers) beyond its far side. After a return to Earth, they will splashdown in the Pacific Ocean, just off the coast of San Diego. Artemis II is a pathfinder mission, designed to test life-support systems, navigation, propulsion, communications and crew operations in deep space. Much like Apollo 8 in 1968, Artemis II is designed to prove that humans can safely travel to lunar distance — an essential prerequisite for landing missions. (L-R) Astronauts Jeremy Hansen, Victor Glover, Reid Wiseman and Christina Hammock Koch stand onstage after being selected for the Artemis II mission who will venture around the Moon during a news conference held by NASA and CSA at Ellington airport in Houston, Texas, on April 3, 2023. - Traveling aboard NASAs Orion spacecraft during Artemis II, the mission is the first crewed flight test on the agencys path to establishing a long-term scientific and human presence on the lunar surface. (Photo by Mark Felix / AFP) (Photo by MARK FELIX/AFP via Getty Images)AFP via Getty ImagesWho Is Flying On Artemis II?Interest in the crew is intense, making who is on the Artemis II crew one of the most searched questions about the mission. NASA has selected four astronauts to travel on the historic flight:Reid Wiseman – CommanderVictor Glover – PilotChristina Koch – Mission SpecialistJeremy Hansen – Mission SpecialistHansen will become the first Canadian and first non-American to travel to lunar distance, while Koch is set to become the first woman to orbit the moon.The Rocket And Spacecraft Powering Artemis IIArtemis II will launch aboard NASA’s Space Launch System, the most powerful rocket ever flown. It’s also one of the most expensive, with NASA reporting the official cost as $23.8 billion. It will launch the Orion deep space capsule (which cost $20.4 billion) and the European Space Agency’s European Service Module (which provides electricity, propulsion, thermal control, air and water). Later missions will also include hardware from Elon Musk’s SpaceX and Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin.When Artemis II Will LaunchNASA currently targets early 2026, with February through April identified as the most likely launch window. The mission will lift off from Kennedy Space Center’s Launch Pad 39B in Florida. “The agency has committed to launch no later than April 2026,” said Lakiesha Hawkins, acting deputy associate administrator at NASA’s Exploration Systems Development Mission Directorate, in September 2025. “Right now, that window could open as early as Feb. 5, depending on how we progress. ”Planned missions of NASA's Artemis program. NASAAll Artemis Missions ExplainedArtemis II fits into a carefully staged sequence of missions designed to move NASA from testing hardware to sustaining human activity on and around the moon. Here’s the full Artemis roadmap:Artemis I (2022) – Uncrewed Orion test flight around the moonArtemis II (2026) – First crewed lunar flybyArtemis III (no earlier than mid-2027) – First crewed moon landing since ApolloArtemis IV – Delivery of a lunar-orbit habitat and surface missionArtemis V And Beyond – Expanded lunar landings, Gateway growth, long-term presenceAn artist’s concept of a suited Artemis astronaut looking out of a Moon lander hatch across the lunar surface, the Lunar Terrain Vehicle, and other surface elements.NASANASA’s Artemis III Mission And What It Will DoArtemis II will determine whether the U.S. can truly return to the moon, but it’s mostly a gateway mission to Artemis III, an ambitious mission to land at least two astronauts on the moon in 2027. A 30-day mission, Artemis III will see two astronauts descend to the moon’s south pole from NASA’s Lunar Gateway space station — which received thrusters last week — in an adapted SpaceX Starship spacecraft. Artemis III will involve three moonwalks in 6.5 days before Starship takes them back to the Lunar Gateway for a transfer to Orion for the trip home to Earth.Will Artemis III ever happen? There’s a lot to be done to make it a reality — both by NASA and SpaceX — but if it stands any chance, Artemis II has to be a success in 2026. Wishing you clear skies and wide eyes.
